title: One Rod Became Two. The Load on One Beam Doubled. Nobody Ever Established Who Changed It.
description:
More like this already exist: this is one of 56 full-length cases on this channel, 28 of them posted in the last 28 days.
More are finished and already scheduled. Subscribing is what puts the next one in front of you:
https://www.youtube.com/@primedocumentarystudio?sub_confirmation=1

On 17 July 1981, at about 7:05 in the evening, between 1,500 and 2,000 people were in the atrium of the year-old Hyatt Regency in Kansas City for the weekly tea dance. The band had come back from its break a minute earlier. Two suspended walkways, at the second and fourth floor levels, came down. Together they weighed 142,000 pounds. The Missouri Court of Appeals put the toll at 114 dead and at least 186 injured; the federal investigation counted 111 killed outright and 188 injured, of whom two subsequently died. It called it the most devastating collapse ever to take place in the United States.

Three walkways crossed the atrium. The third was offset from the other two and hung separately from the roof framing, and it did not fall. The other two shared one system: hanger rods an inch and a quarter across, threaded at each end for a nut and a washer, passing through box beams made from two ordinary eight-inch steel channels welded toe to toe. As designed, a single continuous rod ran from the roof through the fourth-floor beam and on down to the second floor, and each beam handed its own load straight into the rod.

That is not what was built. During construction the fabricator's shop drawings called for two sets of rods: an upper set from the roof to the fourth floor, a lower set from the fourth floor down to the second, offset four inches so they did not share a hole. Because of certain fabricating problems, Havens Steel proposed the double rod to the project engineer, Daniel Duncan. The consequence is one sentence long. All of the second-floor walkway's load was now carried first to the fourth-floor box beam, where it was added to that walkway's own load. The design load at the connection went from about 20 kips to about 41. The federal report's conclusion, stated twice, is a word: doubled.

Somebody did ask. A technician checking the shop drawings raised the change with Duncan, who said the two-rod arrangement was basically the same as the one rod concept. The licensing board later found he had been asked about it on at least six separate occasions during construction, and had assured each inquirer. It was a reasonable inference from the evidence, the Court of Appeals wrote, that he never made the calculations. Duncan and Jack Gillum approved the shop drawings; Gillum's seal was on the structural drawings, and the firm's own procedures required a detailed check of all special connections.

Under the building code the connection should have supported an ultimate load of at least 68 kips. Testing put what they actually had at an average of 18.6. The load on one when it failed was 21.4 kips: 31 percent of the capacity the code expected, and 53 percent of the load it should have been designed for. Bad workmanship and bad steel were excluded, and so was the most persistent myth about that night: dynamic loads from walking or dancing would not have been significant beside the static loads. Nor had the original detail ever been legal — without the change it would still have fallen short of the code; it would simply have held that evening.

No criminal charges were ever filed. In December 1983 the county prosecutor and the US Attorney announced they had found insufficient evidence, and insurers had by then paid over $78,000,000 to settle civil claims. In February 1984 the Missouri licensing board filed a complaint against Duncan, Gillum and their firm. Twenty-seven days of hearing produced a 442-page decision, and in January 1986 all three certificates were revoked. The Court of Appeals affirmed in 1988, reversing a single finding. The rule it rested on is the sentence the case left behind: an engineer may delegate the work of design, but he cannot delegate the responsibility.

Some things were never established. No tribunal determined who first drew the second rod. The original design calculations were never produced, and the board did not investigate the architect or the contractor, who had also stamped the shop drawings. The discipline was not for the deaths: the breach occurred, the court held, when the design was incorporated into the building with their approval, whether or not any collapse subsequently occurred.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic; no real-person likeness is shown, no victim, injury or debris is depicted, and no image is offered as the hotel or its walkways.
National Bureau of Standards, Building Science Series 143 (May 1982). Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988). Pfatteicher, "The Hyatt Horror", J. Performance of Constructed Facilities 14(2).
